item.title: Visual Studio November Update – Faster Workflows, Better Reviews
item.dc:creator: Mark Downie
item.description:
The November Visual Studio update reduces repeated work in large-solution workflows, adds MSBuild Restore in Open Folder, introduces Copilot Chat's new engine and work controls, helps organize large pull-request reviews, and adds CSS color previews and IntelliSense.

The post Visual Studio November Update – Faster Workflows, Better Reviews appeared first on Visual Studio Blog.
item.content:encoded:
Long waits have a way of breaking concentration. Visual Studio now does less repeated work when you open or close large solutions, launch designers and dialogs, and refresh source-control status. In Open Folder, you can also restore MSBuild dependencies without opening a solution first.

The new Copilot Chat is now on by default for eligible accounts. It handles long sessions more smoothly, accepts files dragged directly into a prompt, keeps conversations in their own tabs, and remembers your conversation mode and tool permissions for each session. Copilot also helps when it’s time to review: Change Groups organizes large pull requests into focused groups with summaries and review guidance, so you can see the structure before opening every file. In the CSS editor, color swatches show stylesheet colors as you edit. Get the Visual Studio 2026 Stable Channel and let us know where these changes help you most.

A More Responsive Visual Studio

Visual Studio now does less redundant work when large solutions load and close. Reusing project-directory information when refreshing C++ comment tasks reduced the measured Parse Solution phase by about 20% for Chromium and 9% for Unreal Engine in the PR’s test scenarios. These figures measure that phase only, not total solution-load time. Separately, Visual Studio removes an unused telemetry query during solution opening.

When you close a large solution, Visual Studio no longer rescans every open document for each project and cuts down on repeated file-watch cleanup. Solution Explorer source-control icon refreshes now run in bounded batches, giving the UI time to render in between. Legacy diagnostic providers also do less work when refreshing large Error List result sets.

When you open Add New Item, Visual Studio loads template registrations for the current project family first instead of initializing every registered project type. You keep the same template choices and project-switching behavior. Windows Forms and UWP XAML designers also avoid repeating some setup work. These changes target Windows Forms designer setup overhead, not your form’s initialization code, and UWP XAML designer startup, not every XAML project type.

Restore MSBuild Dependencies in Open Folder

Working from a folder doesn’t mean you have to open a solution before restoring dependencies. In Open Folder, right-click a supported solution or project file and select Restore to run the MSBuild Restore target through the existing folder build-action workflow.

If the project belongs to a discovered solution, Visual Studio keeps restore in that solution’s targeting context. The command doesn’t apply to CMake or other build providers, and it excludes C++ .vcxproj files.

A More Capable Copilot Chat

Copilot Chat in Visual Studio just got a new engine. Starting with Visual Studio 2026 version 18.12, it runs on the Microsoft Copilot SDK developed by GitHub, the same technology powering GitHub Copilot CLI, the GitHub Copilot app, and VS Code. It’s on by default, and it’s a major upgrade: same models, more tasks solved, new ways to work.

Drag files from Solution Explorer or Windows File Explorer into Chat to attach them to a prompt instead of opening them in the editor. This also addresses a request for drag-and-drop file references. You can use the Test agent to generate tests when Copilot and its testing capability are enabled.

Choose Interactive for request-and-response work or Autopilot to let the agent continue until it considers the task complete. Set Manual or Allow all tool permissions independently. With Autopilot and Manual together, tools not configured for automatic approval are rejected instead of waiting for a prompt. Selecting Allow all shows a warning. Visual Studio saves these modes with each session, and Configure Defaults opens the related Chat settings. These controls address a request to retain MCP and mode settings.

The new engine also brings ways of working with Copilot that the previous experience didn’t offer.

Steer it mid-task. You no longer need to wait for Copilot to finish before redirecting it. Type a new instruction and press Enter, and Copilot applies it while it works. Until then, your message shows as Pending, and you can select the X to withdraw it.

See what Copilot actually did. Each step shows its results, not just the attempt. Expand any step to view the output, open it in the editor, or copy the exact command Copilot ran.

Review Pull Requests Faster with Change Groups

Large pull requests can mix features, tests, refactoring, and supporting changes across many files. Change Groups uses GitHub Copilot to organize related changes into focused review units, so you can understand the structure before opening every file.

Each group includes tags, a concise summary, and Review focus guidance. You can reorder groups, track progress across groups and files, move between comments, and review related files together instead of piecing them together from a flat list.

CSS Editing Improvements

Color swatches now appear beside CSS, SCSS, and LESS color values, making it easier to preview stylesheet colors in the editor. Swatches can resolve CSS custom properties, nested var() references and fallbacks, and resolvable SCSS and LESS variables. Select a swatch to see named-color suggestions or open the picker for hex and functional colors.

Updated schema data adds IntelliSense for modern CSS areas including anchor positioning, animations, fonts, masking, scroll animations, view transitions, and more. Media-query completion suggests feature names and values suited to each feature.

From our entire team, thank you for choosing Visual Studio! For the latest updates, resources, and news, check out the Visual Studio Hub and stay in touch.

Happy coding! The Visual Studio team

The post Visual Studio November Update – Faster Workflows, Better Reviews appeared first on Visual Studio Blog.

item.title: Beyond the prompt: Discovering trusted technical perspectives with your Visual Studio subscription
item.dc:creator: James Rempt
item.description:
AI is changing the speed at which developers can produce code. And with this change, a different challenge emerges: how do we ensure that what we’re building is secure, reliable, and maintainable? Not just an immediate answer AI-generated code can look convincing, compile successfully, and even pass critical tests without necessarily meeting an application’s security, […]

The post Beyond the prompt: Discovering trusted technical perspectives with your Visual Studio subscription appeared first on Visual Studio Blog.
item.content:encoded:
AI is changing the speed at which developers can produce code. And with this change, a different challenge emerges: how do we ensure that what we’re building is secure, reliable, and maintainable?

Not just an immediate answer

AI-generated code can look convincing, compile successfully, and even pass critical tests without necessarily meeting an application’s security, maintainability, or architectural requirements.

A passing test may confirm that an implementation produces the expected result without establishing whether the test adequately covers the requirements, edge cases, or failure conditions. When AI generates both the implementation and its tests, there’s also a risk that the tests reinforce assumptions in the generated code rather than independently validate the intended behavior.

And the challenge extends beyond identifying errors. AI can suggest a technically plausible solution without accounting for every constraint or requirement of the application where it will be used. This means developers need to evaluate the assumptions behind an implementation and understand potential tradeoffs.

These considerations aren’t just limited to AI-generated code. Whether you’re evaluating a new framework, choosing an architecture, or modernizing an existing application, having trusted technical perspectives beyond the immediate implementation guidance is crucial.

Keeping engineering judgment in the process

One way to address this challenge is to apply proven development practices that have been adapted to the rapidly changing technological landscape. That includes meaningful code reviews, the right kind of testing, and clear architectural expectations.

In his CODE Magazine article “AI-Assisted Development Without Losing Engineering Discipline” Sonu Kapoor explores how teams can put these practices to work. He examines how developers can take advantage of AI-assisted coding while maintaining responsibility for the quality of what they build.

Kapoor offers practical guidance on making engineering discipline part of the AI-assisted development process. For example, he recommends establishing shared instructions that communicate a team’s architectural standards and development conventions to AI tools. He also explores how code reviews need to evolve when developers may not have written every line themselves, and why AI-generated tests should validate expected behavior rather than simply confirm the generated implementation.

These are just a few of the considerations he explores as AI becomes part of everyday development. It’s a worthwhile read for anyone looking to make AI-assisted development more productive without losing sight of essential quality controls.

Explore more with CODE Magazine

Kapoor’s article is just one example of the kinds of technical perspectives you can expect to find through CODE Magazine.

In Azure Well-Architected Framework in Practice, Vaibhav Gujral examines the tradeoffs developers and architects face when designing applications for Azure. For example, deploying an application across multiple regions can improve reliability and disaster recovery capabilities, but it also increases costs. Understanding an application’s recovery requirements helps teams determine whether that additional investment makes sense.

CODE Magazine also gives developers opportunities to learn from real-world project experiences. Its Postmortems article series examines what worked, what didn’t, and the lessons developers took away, offering perspectives that can inform decisions in their own work.

And it covers a range of technologies, including C#, .NET, Azure, and AI, alongside topics that speak to security, application architecture, and development practices.

The value goes beyond learning how to use a particular technology. CODE Magazine’s content provides an opportunity to explore different approaches, examine engineering decisions, and consider up to date practices that may be useful in your own projects.

CODE Magazine: A Visual Studio Subscription benefit

If you’re an eligible Visual Studio subscriber, you already have access to this kind of content through your Subscription.

Eligible Visual Studio Professional and Enterprise subscribers can receive a one-year CODE Magazine subscription, with the option to choose print or digital formats. Dev Essentials members have access to the digital version.

It’s an opportunity to explore technical articles, discover different perspectives, and stay current with developments in a variety of technical approaches that matter to your work.

Activate your CODE Magazine benefit

If you haven’t explored this benefit yet, here’s how to get started.

Visit the Visual Studio Subscriber Benefits portal, find CODE Magazine under Professional Development, and select Activate. From there, you can choose your preferred format and complete the subscription process.

Thanks for being part of the Visual Studio community!

The CODE Magazine benefit is nonrenewable. International shipping charges may apply to print editions. You can review the CODE Magazine benefit documentation for eligibility details.

The post Beyond the prompt: Discovering trusted technical perspectives with your Visual Studio subscription appeared first on Visual Studio Blog.

item.title: Live technical training, wherever you are: A VSLive! benefit for Visual Studio subscribers
item.dc:creator: James Rempt
item.description:
Developers are constantly speaking to me about how AI tool mastery has become an essential part of their everyday work. But learning how to use these tools effectively takes more than experimenting with a few prompts, and it often requires opportunities to learn that go beyond documentation and tutorials. Some of the best technical skill development takes […]

The post Live technical training, wherever you are: A VSLive! benefit for Visual Studio subscribers appeared first on Visual Studio Blog.
item.content:encoded:
Developers are constantly speaking to me about how AI tool mastery has become an essential part of their everyday work. But learning how to use these tools effectively takes more than experimenting with a few prompts, and it often requires opportunities to learn that go beyond documentation and tutorials.

Some of the best technical skill development takes place when you can learn directly from an experienced practitioner why they chose one approach over another.

Sure, documentation can explain how a technology is supposed to work. But when you’re evaluating key architectural decisions, working through unfamiliar tools, or trying to discern the downstream implications of the choices you are making, having an opportunity to ask questions and explore different approaches can make a huge difference.

Live virtual training can bring that kind of opportunity to developers wherever they work, so they can get real experience through expert-led, interactive learning environments.

A better way to explore technical challenges

Consider this: you’re working with an existing .NET application, and your team is working to determine how AI coding agents could help modernize it. You’re evaluating unique dependencies, architecture, testing requirements, and security considerations.

The interesting questions aren’t necessarily related to which commands to run. They’re more about what needs closer examination and how to plan for the work required.

Or perhaps you’re designing an Azure application and evaluating different approaches to scalability, performance, and cost. While tutorials can help explain available services and architectural patterns, applying those approaches to your own requirements often involves balancing competing priorities.

That’s where an instructor-led virtual workshop can offer something special.

Instead of simply seeing a technical solution in action, you can explore how an experienced instructor approaches the problem, understand the reasoning behind technical decisions, and ask questions about the alternatives.

Explore VSLive! virtual training

VSLive! offers live virtual technical training throughout the year, covering a variety of development technologies and topics.

These live virtual trainings vary from focused two-day workshops to multi-day technical deep dives and courses delivered over several weeks.

Here are a few upcoming examples:

  • Immersive .NET Full Stack Training with Copilot (December 15–18, 2026): Spend four days building applications that connect the different layers of the .NET stack, from data access to web interfaces. You’ll come away with hands-on experience using these technologies together, along with new ways to incorporate GitHub Copilot into your development workflow.
  • Modernizing Legacy .NET Applications with AI Coding Agents (January 28–29, 2027): Work through the challenges of modernizing an older .NET application while exploring where AI coding agents can help. You’ll leave with a practical modernization approach, assessment templates, and reusable resources you can adapt to your own projects.
  • Mastering Microsoft Foundry: From First Agent to Production (February 4 – March 11, 2027): Follow the development of an AI agent from initial implementation through evaluation, monitoring, and security review. You’ll gain a clearer understanding of the decisions involved in preparing agents for production, with dedicated office hours to discuss questions and challenges.

These programs represent just a few of the available learning opportunities. Visit the VSLive! Virtual Training calendar to explore additional topics and upcoming sessions.

Your Visual Studio Subscription can help

Eligible Visual Studio subscribers can access VSLive! event discounts of up to $900 off standard event pricing for both virtual training and in-person conferences. If you’re considering technical training, it’s worth checking out.

Visit the Visual Studio Subscriber Portal to review your available VSLive! benefit and claim your discount code. Then explore the virtual training calendar to find a program that aligns with your interests.

Thanks for being part of the Visual Studio community!

Savings vary by event; check the offer in your Subscriber Portal before registering.

item.description:

Then came another request from management: Could they add a dashboard within the app so users could actually see what was happening with all that data? […]

item.content:encoded:
I was talking with a developer recently about a project his team was working on. They’d built an application, connected their data sources, and had everything in working order. Then came another request from management: Could they add a dashboard within the app so users could actually see what was happening with all that data?

As we talked, the developer explained what that really meant. More infrastructure, more queries, more charts, additional reporting functionality, and another set of features to build, test and maintain. And all of this would take valuable time to produce.

Sound familiar?

It’s a common challenge. The data is already there, but turning it into something useful in your app can become a project of its own.

If that resonates, now is a good time to explore your Visual Studio subscriber benefits.

Eligible Visual Studio Professional and Enterprise subscribers have access to the Bold BI Cloud Edition benefit from Syncfusion. It’s designed to help developers create interactive dashboards, connect data sources, and bring analytics into their applications without building everything bit by bit. Once activated, this subscriber benefit is provided at no additional cost for a 6-month period, providing an opportunity to explore and experiment as you test and build the reporting solutions that work best for you.

Turn your data into something useful

Valuable applications should generate valuable data. The challenge is not only making that information accessible and meaningful to the people who need it, but also making it visible in the places that can add the most value.

Perhaps a product manager wants to understand how customers use a particular feature. Or maybe a sales team needs a practical revenue operations dashboard to monitor pipeline and conversions. You could build the required reporting experience yourself, including the systems architecture, data connections, visualizations, and dashboard interfaces. But before committing significant time and resources to building a solution from scratch, it’s worth exploring how Bold BI Cloud Edition can help create those dashboards and embed them directly into your application. With 6 months of Bold BI through your subscriber benefit, you have time to experiment with the available reporting solutions.

 

And with AI-powered insights, you have another way to explore the data behind those dashboards and uncover information that might otherwise take additional analysis. It’s a practical way to extend what your applications can do while keeping your attention on the development work that matters most.

Bring powerful analytics into your development workflow

With Bold BI Cloud Edition, developers can:

  • Connect to 140+ data sources: Bring information together from databases, cloud platforms, and business applications without building every integration from scratch.
  • Build interactive dashboards: Create charts, graphs, tables, and other visualizations using an interactive dashboard editor.
  • Embed analytics into applications: Add dashboards directly into applications, giving users access to insights within their existing workflows.
  • Explore AI-powered insights: Use AI-assisted capabilities to better understand connected data and identify useful trends.
  • Share insights with others: Collaborate with team members and stakeholders through dashboards, scheduled exports, and email sharing.

Bold BI also includes onboarding services to help subscribers get started with this benefit.

Put your subscriber benefit to work

One of the things I appreciate about Visual Studio Subscriptions is that the value extends well beyond the IDE. Your Subscription can include developer tools, cloud services, training resources, and partner benefits designed to help you build, learn, and work more efficiently.

Bold BI is one of those benefits you may not have explored yet.

If you’re considering a way to bring analytics into your applications without building everything yourself, your 6 months of Bold BI Cloud Edition is worth exploring. Go to https://my.visualstudio.com/ to learn more. And when you’re ready to test a reporting experience in your next app, that’s the perfect time to consider activating your Bold BI benefit through the Visual Studio Subscriptions portal.

item.title: Bring Your Own Model is now generally available in Visual Studio
item.dc:creator: Praveen Sethuraman
item.description:
Whether your team hosts its own AI models, you have an API key from a model provider, or you want to experiment with a model running on your machine, Bring Your Own Model (BYOM) lets you use those models without leaving Visual Studio. BYOM is now generally available in Visual Studio 18.12. Since the August […]

The post Bring Your Own Model is now generally available in Visual Studio appeared first on Visual Studio Blog.
item.content:encoded:
Whether your team hosts its own AI models, you have an API key from a model provider, or you want to experiment with a model running on your machine, Bring Your Own Model (BYOM) lets you use those models without leaving Visual Studio.

BYOM is now generally available in Visual Studio 18.12. Since the August Preview, your feedback has shaped improvements for team deployments, enterprise networks, and personal projects. This release brings multiple configurations for the same provider, a dedicated custom-endpoint experience that includes local models, more control over API compatibility, and improved proxy support.

No GitHub sign-in is required. If you can’t access GitHub, you can still use your chosen models in Visual Studio—including local or internally hosted models in air-gapped environments—provided the model endpoint is reachable and its authentication requirements are met.

More than one connection to the same provider

Your work doesn’t always fit into a single provider configuration. You might use one account for personal projects and another for work, connect to separate Microsoft Foundry resources, or keep an experimental deployment alongside your team’s approved endpoint.

You can now keep multiple configurations for the same provider and give them meaningful names, such as “Work” and “Personal.” Each keeps its own connection details and models, so you can choose the right setup without removing and re-adding a provider.

A clearer path to custom endpoints

Many developers don’t connect directly to a model vendor’s public endpoint. You might use a self-hosted inference server, an AI gateway, or an endpoint provided by your organization.

The new Custom Endpoint provider gives OpenAI-compatible services, including OpenRouter, their own place in provider configuration. Enter your endpoint URL and an API key if required. Where the endpoint provides a compatible model listing, Visual Studio can surface the models it returns.

You can also connect to local models served by LM Studio. Start the local server, then add its OpenAI-compatible URL using Custom Endpoint to use your model in Visual Studio’s Agent Mode.

Match the API to your model

When adding a custom model, you can now select the API format supported by your provider: OpenAI-compatible Completions or Responses, or Anthropic-compatible Messages. You can also view and change the configured format in Manage models

You can also configure context size, maximum output, tool calling, and vision support to match your model and deployment.

Better suited to enterprise environments

For organizations, model choice needs to work with existing network settings and policies.

We’ve improved proxy support so provider connections and Agent Mode both use Visual Studio’s resolved proxy configuration.

Administrators can enable or disable BYOM through organizational policy.

Getting Started

Try BYOM in Visual Studio:

  1. Install Visual Studio 18.12 GA.
  2. Open Chat and use the model picker to choose Manage models.
  3. Choose Add model provider, then select Microsoft Foundry, OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, or Custom Endpoint.
  4. Configure the connection, give it a meaningful name, and add the models you want to use.
  5. Select your model and start working in Agent Mode.

Note: If you don’t see Add model provider, your organization’s administrator may have disabled bring-your-own-model access.

Keep shaping what comes next

We’re continuing to learn from the models, deployments, and environments you use. Tell us what’s working, where setup still gets in your way, and what would make BYOM more useful through the Developer Community forum or our short survey.

Your feedback is helping shape what comes next. Happy coding!

The post Bring Your Own Model is now generally available in Visual Studio appeared first on Visual Studio Blog.

item.title: Announcing Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11
item.dc:creator: Jamshed Damkewala
item.description:
Today, we are announcing Visual Studio 2026 Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) 18.11 alongside Visual Studio 2026 18.12 on the Stable channel. LTSC 18.11 will receive two years of support, through November 14, 2028, rather than the one year of LTSC support we previously announced. If you are using Visual Studio 2022 for its LTSC benefits […]

The post Announcing Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11 appeared first on Visual Studio Blog.
item.content:encoded:
Today, we are announcing Visual Studio 2026 Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) 18.11 alongside Visual Studio 2026 18.12 on the Stable channel. LTSC 18.11 will receive two years of support, through November 14, 2028, rather than the one year of LTSC support we previously announced. If you are using Visual Studio 2022 for its LTSC benefits this is a great time to consider migrating to the new Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11 to get the latest Visual Studio has to offer.

Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11 is not a new product – it is a new support and servicing channel for Visual Studio 2026 so it includes the full feature set, capabilities, and fixes as Visual Studio 2026 18.0 through 18.10. If you have stayed on Visual Studio 2022 while waiting for a Visual Studio 2026 LTSC release with LTS toolsets, you should begin planning validation and deployment of LTSC 18.11.

View the Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11 Release Notes

We are not changing how the Stable channel works. Stable will continue receiving monthly feature and quality updates. If you are on Stable and want to keep receiving those updates, you do not need to change anything. LTSC is an option if your organization needs to stay on a fixed release.

Why are we making this change?

In November 2025, we announced a new release and support model with Visual Studio 2026, including one year on Stable followed by one year of LTSC support. Customers told us that one year of LTSC support did not leave enough time to validate and deploy a release. The longer support period gives those organizations more time to deploy and use LTSC 18.11.

An LTSC release with LTS toolsets

Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11 will include Long-Term Support (LTS) toolsets for .NET and C++ development: .NET 10 LTS and MSVC 14.50 and 14.52. The MSVC and .NET toolsets in Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11 will be supported per their respective support lifecycles, which are at least as long as the support lifecycle for Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11.

Stable is for feature updates and servicing, we recommend this as the default

Stable remains the recommended channel if you want the latest Visual Studio features, including new GitHub Copilot capabilities. To remain supported on Stable, keep your installation current with its monthly updates. Stable is where most customers will be and we strongly recommend this channel so you can receive and take advantage of the latest features Visual Studio has to offer.

LTSC will get servicing only

LTSC 18.11 will receive security and other critical fixes, we do not plan to ship regular feature updates for LTSC like we will for the Stable cannel. If you choose LTSC to limit feature changes in your development environment, you still need to keep your installation current with LTSC servicing updates to remain supported.

Existing Visual Studio 2026 keys continue to work

Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11 is not a new product, the product remains Visual Studio 2026. Today’s announcement is a new channel for the existing product. Therefore, existing Visual Studio 2026 product keys will continue to work on both Stable and LTSC 18.11 for Enterprise, Professional, and the Build Tools SKUs. You do not need a new key or another purchase of Visual Studio 2026 to use either channel.

Getting started

If your organization has stayed on Visual Studio 2022 while waiting for a Visual Studio 2026 LTSC release with LTS toolsets, you should begin planning validation and deployment of LTSC 18.11.

Before deployment, review Visual Studio Product Lifecycle and Servicing for support requirements and installation and deployment guidance. Refer to this guidance for information about Switching between Stable and LTSC channels. You can find more details about this release in the Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11 release notes.

The post Announcing Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11 appeared first on Visual Studio Blog.

item.title: Copilot in Visual Studio Just Got a Major Upgrade
item.dc:creator: Dalia Abo Sheasha
item.description:
Copilot Chat in Visual Studio just got a new engine. Starting with Visual Studio 2026 version 18.12, it runs on the Microsoft Copilot SDK developed by GitHub, the same technology powering GitHub Copilot CLI, the GitHub Copilot app, and VS Code. It’s on by default, and it’s a major upgrade: same models, more tasks solved, […]

The post Copilot in Visual Studio Just Got a Major Upgrade appeared first on Visual Studio Blog.
item.content:encoded:
Copilot Chat in Visual Studio just got a new engine. Starting with Visual Studio 2026 version 18.12, it runs on the Microsoft Copilot SDK developed by GitHub, the same technology powering GitHub Copilot CLI, the GitHub Copilot app, and VS Code. It’s on by default, and it’s a major upgrade: same models, more tasks solved, new ways to work.

We put the previous and new Copilot experiences through over one hundred coding tasks. The new experience came out ahead with every model we tested, across capability levels and providers, resolving up to 21 more tasks.

The chat itself is better too: you get shorter, more focused answers, you can steer Copilot mid-task and see what each request costs.

More Tasks Solved

To measure what matters to .NET developers, the .NET team built a benchmark from real issues in real C# projects, across .NET Framework and .NET Core, Azure and Aspire, and WinForms and desktop apps. We ran both Copilot chat experiences through 157 of its tasks. A task counts as resolved only when its failing tests pass without breaking any that already passed.

The new engine has also been tested on C++, Python, and a range of other languages.

One example from our own backlog: a user reported that long answer choices in Copilot’s questions were getting cut off. We asked Copilot to help reproduce it, once in the previous experience and once in the new SDK-powered experience. The previous experience came back with steps for us to reproduce it by hand. The new one did something we didn’t expect: it realized it was running inside the very chat window that had the bug, so it reproduced the problem right there.

Same Models, Better Harness

On its own, a model reads text and writes text. It can’t open your solution, edit a file, or run your tests. The harness is everything around the model that turns text into real work: what the model sees, which tools it can use, what it remembers, and what it’s allowed to touch. Give the same model a better harness, and you get better results.

Through the SDK, Copilot in Visual Studio now runs on the Microsoft Copilot harness. It’s battle-tested at the scale of millions of users, and GitHub designed it to be fast and predictable. Here’s what you’ll notice:

  • It finishes the job. The harness keeps Copilot going until the task is actually done.
  • It gets to the point. One developer described the experience as “Less chatter, more quality results for large tasks”.

New in Copilot Chat

The new engine also changes how you work with Copilot. Here’s what you won’t find in the previous experience.

  • Steer it while it works. No more waiting for Copilot to finish before you change course. Type a new instruction and press Enter, and Copilot picks it up mid-task. Until it does, your message is marked Pending, and you can select the X to take it back.

  • See what Copilot actually did. Every step shows what came back, not just what Copilot tried. Expand a step to see the results, open them in the editor, or copy the exact command Copilot ran.
  • Watch subagents at work. When Copilot hands off part of a task to a subagent, the subagent gets its own card showing which model it’s using and every step it takes, live.

  • Work beyond your solution. Point Copilot at any folder on your machine from the chat header or attach whole folders as context.

  • Get a second opinion. With Agent selected, type / to call on one of the built-in agents. /security-review runs a security-focused review of your changes to find vulnerabilities, and /rubber-duck has a different model critique Copilot’s plan before it acts.

Still Unmistakably Visual Studio

Because it’s the same technology, Copilot behaves more consistently across Visual Studio, VS Code, Copilot CLI, and the GitHub Copilot app. Write an agent skill once, and it works in all four without modifications. Improve the harness, and every surface benefits.

But the same engine doesn’t mean a one-size-fits-all experience. Copilot still works with the tools you rely on in Visual Studio. Specialized agents help you debug, profile, fix build failures, modernize .NET apps, and speed up C++ builds. Built-in agent skills add .NET and Azure expertise, alongside the MCP servers you’ve already set up.

Try It Today

Update to Visual Studio 2026 version 18.12, open Copilot Chat, and give it a task from your own backlog. That bug you’ve been putting off? Start there.

We’re still bringing over a few features from the previous experience, like plan mode and chat exports. If you rely on them, or need to switch back for any reason, you can turn off “Use new Copilot chat experience” in Tools > Options > GitHub > Copilot > Copilot Chat, restart Visual Studio, and please take some time to tell us why.

Tell us what Copilot gets right and where it needs to improve. Report issues through Help > Send Feedback > Report a Problem, or share your ideas on Developer Community.

Happy coding!

The post Copilot in Visual Studio Just Got a Major Upgrade appeared first on Visual Studio Blog.

item.content:encoded:
Keeping up with new technology is one thing. Finding worthwhile opportunities to explore what matters most to your work is another.

That’s where VSLive! can help. It brings technical learning, hands-on experience, expert guidance, and a community of developers together in one place, giving you focused time to explore evolving technologies and decide what’s worth bringing back to your team.

And if you’re an eligible Dev Essentials member, Visual Studio Professional subscriber, or Visual Studio Enterprise subscriber, you have benefits that can provide a significant discount for these in-person events.

Develop skills you can put to work

One of the things that makes VSLive! so beneficial is its focus on practical learning. Rather than simply hearing about the latest technologies, developers have opportunities to explore how those technologies can help solve real development challenges.

For example, if you’re interested in furthering your skills with Copilot, VSlive! Las Vegas 2027 will offer a dedicated hands on lab equipping you to build an ASP.NET Core Web Assembly SPA from scratch (all in just one day).

Maybe you’d like to witness Microsoft Foundry in action. VSLive! Las Vegas 2027 will also include dedicated session time for a practical tour of Foundry through the lifecycle of an AI agent. This session will show how Toolbox connects agents to services and tools, how Foundry IQ grounds to enterprise knowledge, and how Hosted Agents support custom agents.

If you’re struggling with the growing menu of AI coding tools and looking for a framework to compare your many options, you’ll love the demo driven AI comparison session. During this session, major AI contenders will be contrasted side by side as they work to accomplish the same tasks. You’ll see for yourself which tools are best suited for the challenges you face everyday and come away with practical insights.

Learn from the people around you

Some of the most valuable opportunities at VSLive! happen outside the scheduled sessions.

Think about the last time you tried to work through a new technical problem on your own. Chances are another developer has encountered something similar, and at VSLive!, you can connect with developers facing many of the same challenges, compare experiences, discuss solutions, and discover approaches you might not have considered. A conversation between sessions could introduce you to a useful tool, a better development practice, or a different way of solving a problem.

There’s also value in learning directly from the people who work with these technologies every day. Attendees often have the chance to interact with Microsoft product team members, ask questions about the tools they use, and share feedback based on the latest industry changes.

Those conversations can create opportunities for two-way learning. Developers gain additional insight into the critical technologies they depend on, while our product team can hear directly about real-world challenges and experiences.

It’s this combination of technical learning, shared experience, and community that makes VSLive! more than just a collection of conference sessions.

Save up to $900 with your Visual Studio Subscription

Here’s a benefit worth checking before making your conference plans: Subscribers can receive discounts of up to $900 on VSLive! conference registration through their Visual Studio Subscription.

It’s another way your Subscription can help you stay ahead of the curve and take advantage of learning opportunities beyond the software, cloud services, and training resources you may already be using.

Looking ahead to VSLive! in 2027

As you consider investing in your technical skills next year, several VSLive! events are already scheduled for 2027:

  • VSLive! Las Vegas | March 22–26, 2027
  • VSLive! Austin | May 2–6, 2027
  • VSLive! at Microsoft HQ | August 2–6, 2027

If you’re an eligible Dev Essentials member or Visual Studio subscriber, visit the Visual Studio Subscriber Portal to redeem your VSLive! benefit. Join the community at VSLive! and realize what thousands of developers already have: there’s no place like VSLive! to sharpen your skillset, get practical experience, and solve for the challenges you face every day.

item.content:encoded:
Are you thinking about earning a Microsoft certification to help advance your career, build on your existing skills, or meet new requirements at work?

If so, you may already be wondering where to start. Which courses, labs, and hands-on exercises will help you prepare? How much time will it take to find the right resources, and how much will that training cost?

Here’s something you may not be aware of: Eligible Visual Studio Subscriptions already include many of the learning resources you need to prepare for your next certification.

Visual Studio subscribers can access training from Cloud Academy and Pluralsight, including certification-focused courses, structured learning paths, and hands-on labs that can help you build your skills and prepare for certification exams.

Let’s look at a few ways you can put those benefits to work.

Interested in AI-powered applications?

If Microsoft Certified: Azure AI Apps and Agents Developer is a certification you’re considering, your subscriber benefits can provide a useful starting point preparing for the required AI-103 exam.

For developers looking to build AI skills, preparing for AI-103 offers an opportunity to learn how to develop generative AI applications, integrate AI services, and create intelligent agents and workflows.

Pluralsight offers AI-103-aligned learning resources that can help you work through relevant concepts and build your knowledge of AI applications and agents.

Preparing for Azure administration?

If you want to be a Microsoft Certified: Azure Administrator Associate, your Visual Studio Subscription learning benefits can help you get ready for the necessary AZ-104 exam.

Whether you’re new to Azure administration or looking to strengthen your existing skills, preparing for AZ-104 can help you develop practical knowledge of virtual networks, storage, compute resources, and identity management.

Cloud Academy and Pluralsight offer AZ-104 training, helping you focus on relevant administration skills through in-depth coursework and learning experiences.

Hoping to develop a higher level of cloud architecture expertise?

If you’re Interested in becoming a Microsoft Certified: Azure Solutions Architect Expert, preparing for the required AZ-305 exam can help you strengthen your skills in designing Azure solutions for infrastructure, security, data storage, and business continuity.

Pluralsight and Cloud Academy offer training aligned with the AZ-305 exam requirements, providing additional resources to study Azure architecture concepts as you work toward your certification goals.

Note: To become a Microsoft Certified: Azure Solutions Architect Expert, you must earn the Microsoft Certified: Azure Administrator Associate certification.

Put what you’re learning into practice

Courses are a useful starting point, but applying what you’ve learned can help reinforce new skills.

Your Visual Studio Subscription provides opportunities to do both. Pluralsight and Cloud Academy offer guided labs, technical courses, and practical learning experiences that can help you work with Azure technologies as you study. Beyond just providing content to study, they provide hands-on, practical application labs that allow you to grow your skills actively, with added support from AI powered learning assistants.

And if your Subscription includes Azure monthly credits, you can use eligible Azure services to explore configurations, test ideas, and practice skills in a development environment. These opportunities can help you move beyond just reading about a technology and help you actually start working with it.

Start preparing for your next certification with your Subscription benefits

These are just several examples of the opportunities your Visual Studio Subscription provides. If you’re considering furthering your career, honing your technical skills, or meeting new professional requirements, you have a solid starting point through your Subscription benefits.

Visit the Visual Studio Subscriptions portal to activate your eligible Cloud Academy and Pluralsight benefits and start preparing with learning resources aligned to your certification goals. Begin making progress toward your next certification today with the learning paths and hands-on resources you already have.

Note: Learning benefit availability, eligibility, access duration, and course selection vary by Visual Studio Subscription. Specific training content may change or may not be included in every subscriber benefit offering. Certification exams and exam fees are separate from the learning benefits described here unless otherwise specified. Visit Professional and Technical Credentials and Certifications | Microsoft Learn for more information on certifications and requirements.

The post Preparing for your next certification could start with your Visual Studio Subscription appeared first on Visual Studio Blog.

item.title: Visual Studio October Update – Compare Commits to Your Code, Resolve Conflicts in Bulk, Keep Coding
item.dc:creator: Mark Downie
item.description:
Compare commits with your working tree, resolve merge conflicts in bulk, and keep coding with refreshed Copilot chat, Hot Exit, keyboard tab controls, and Fonts and Colors.

The post Visual Studio October Update – Compare Commits to Your Code, Resolve Conflicts in Bulk, Keep Coding appeared first on Visual Studio Blog.
item.content:encoded:
The October Visual Studio update gives you a clearer view of how your code has changed and more control over resolving merge conflicts. Compare an earlier commit directly with your current working tree, including edits still in progress, and apply the same conflict resolution across multiple files at once.

There’s more to try beyond Git: a new Copilot chat experience, Hot Exit for unfinished work, keyboard shortcuts for organizing tabs, and a refreshed Fonts and Colors page. Update to the Visual Studio 2026 Stable Channel to get started.

Compare a Commit to Your Working Tree

Need to see how your current code differs from an earlier commit? You can now compare that commit directly with your working tree across your repository, including committed changes and edits still in progress. Use it to review a refactor across several commits or investigate what’s changed since a known-good version.

From commit history or the branch list in the Git Repository window, right-click a commit and select Compare with Working Tree. The compare view lets you browse changed files and inspect their diffs against the code you have today.

Bulk Resolve Merge Conflicts

When you already know which side to keep across several conflicted files, you shouldn’t have to repeat that choice for every file. You can now resolve conflicts across a group of files at once.

In Git Changes, right-click multiple selected files, a folder, or the repository root under Unmerged Changes and select Keep All Current or Take All Incoming. The selected resolution applies to all selected files, or all conflicted files within the selected folder or repository.

Try the New Copilot Chat Experience

The new GitHub Copilot Chat experience builds on the Copilot SDK foundation introduced with Agent (Preview). That foundation now extends to Ask mode, Agent mode, and the underlying chat infrastructure, sharing the SDK used by the Copilot CLI and GitHub Copilot app.

It brings more capable end-to-end agent workflows with less back-and-forth, longer-running sessions with more effective prompt caching, and consistent behavior across Copilot experiences. To try it, open Tools > Options > GitHub > Copilot > Copilot Chat, select Use new Copilot chat experience, then restart Visual Studio.

Enable it for your next coding session and let us know how it handles the work. If something is missing or isn’t working, use Help > Send Feedback > Report a Problem to tell us.

Keep Unsaved Work with Hot Exit

Closing Visual Studio doesn’t have to mean deciding where to save every unfinished file. Hot Exit preserves your unsaved work between sessions, including new files you haven’t saved and edits to existing files.

When you reopen Visual Studio, it restores those documents and changes, along with your tab and window layout. It also preserves undo functionality for saved files, including Ctrl+Z. Hot Exit is off by default; to enable it, open Tools > Options, expand All Settings > Projects and Solutions > General, and select Reopen unsaved documents on solution load or empty environment.

Move Documents with the Keyboard

You can now reorder tabs without reaching for the mouse. Press Ctrl+Shift+PgUp to move the active tab left or Ctrl+Shift+PgDn to move it right. With vertical tabs, the same shortcuts move it up or down. They work for documents and tool windows hosted in the document well.

Pinned and unpinned tabs stay separate. Vertical tabs stay within their project group, and manual reordering isn’t available when alphabetical sorting is enabled. Preview tabs can’t be moved.

You can remap Window.MoveTabLeft and Window.MoveTabRight in Tools > Options > Environment > Keyboard. The defaults replace the previous Text Editor bindings for Edit.ViewTopExtend and Edit.ViewBottomExtend; those commands remain available if you want to assign them different shortcuts.

Personalize Fonts and Colors

Finding the right editor customization is easier with the refreshed Fonts and Colors experience, now built on Unified Settings. Category-based navigation and integrated search help you find the settings you want, while inline previews let you see colors and font styles alongside each item.

Foreground colors, background colors, font styles, and previews are all displayed in the settings grid, so you can review and update multiple items without repeatedly selecting each one. Changes also stay synchronized with settings.json, giving you a way to inspect, edit, share, or revert your customizations directly in the file.

From our entire team, thank you for choosing Visual Studio! For the latest updates, resources, and news, check out the Visual Studio Hub and stay in touch.

Happy coding! The Visual Studio team

The post Visual Studio October Update – Compare Commits to Your Code, Resolve Conflicts in Bulk, Keep Coding appeared first on Visual Studio Blog.
